mappings.note: Retrieval of the sum the postmaster managed to raise (70 pesos). A stated fact, so LO-1, not the motive question that would be LO-2.
Literal retrieval of a number from the Mandela text (two deputy presidents). Whatever prose it belongs to, the skill is extracting a stated fact, which is LO-1.
Mandela's claim that the oppressor is no freer than the oppressed is the writer's message, named in LO-2; LO-1 would reduce it to a lookup.
Asks what the title is built on - titling is a literary convention, and no LO in this frame covers it.
A distance stated in the narrative. Plain extraction of information, so LO-1.
Where the girls waited for Wanda is a stated detail of setting; retrieval, hence LO-1 rather than character analysis.
Identifying the tone of a character's reply means reading her state of mind in context - LO-2, not the fact-finding LO-1.
'Fire and Ice' is the poem set with this chapter; the item asks what fire is compared with, i.e. recognising the poem's figure. Figurative language falls under C-E1.4 and under none of the LOs.
How the narrator went about befriending Anil is narrated directly; the answer is extracted, not inferred, so LO-1.
Name of the shop below Anil's room - a single stated detail. LO-1.
Straight word-meaning item for 'jostling'. Vocabulary is named in C-E1.1; C-E1.3 covers grammar, which is not at issue.
Requires inferring the passage's point about why humans are not robots. Inferring and interpreting an unseen passage is C-E1.1, not a literature outcome.
Identifying the tone of a quoted sentence from a non-fiction passage is interpretation of the writer's stance - C-E1.1. The literary outcomes are about the prescribed texts.
Tests correct use of 'grit' in a new sentence, i.e. word meaning in context. Vocabulary sits in C-E1.1; it is a usage choice, not a grammar rule, so not C-E1.3.
Comprehension of what the passage prescribes for developing perseverance - decoding and inferring, C-E1.1.
Asks for the message of the closing paragraph, i.e. the central idea of a prose extract, which is exactly LO-1. Not C-E1.1, which covers word-level and sentence-level decoding.
Literal meaning of the term 'Renaissance' - a vocabulary item, C-E1.1.
Retrieval of what the passage reports about the Renaissance period; information extraction from a prose extract, LO-1, rather than the word-meaning sibling C-E1.1.
Synonym selection for 'inquisitiveness'. Vocabulary, C-E1.1.
First blank of a letter-to-the-editor layout task; what is marked is correct letter format, which C-E1.2 names. Not C-E1.3, because no grammatical structure is tested.
Second blank of the same letter-to-the-editor format task, so the same format-and-tone outcome applies.
Third blank of the letter-to-the-editor format task; format of a written piece, C-E1.2.
Fourth blank of the letter-to-the-editor format task; grouped with its siblings under the writing-format outcome.
Gap-fill in a note about the Wangala festival where the missing item is a verb/article form. Grammatical accuracy, so C-E1.3, not comprehension.
Second blank of the same gap-fill; the choice is a connective/prepositional form, a grammar decision.
Third blank of the gap-fill, requiring the correct verb form for the leading warrior. Grammatical convention, C-E1.3.
Fourth blank of the gap-fill, a subject-verb agreement/tense choice. C-E1.3.
Setting detail from the story's opening line; extraction, LO-1.
The earth needed only a downpour - a fact stated in the text. LO-1, not the imagery competency, since no figure is being recognised.
Direction of the approaching clouds (north-east) is a stated detail. LO-1.
Corn is named in the story; single-fact retrieval, LO-1.
The hailstorm as the agent of ruin is stated in the narrative; extraction rather than inference.
Completes the story's simile - the field 'as if covered in salt'. Recognising the comparison is a literary-convention skill, which only C-E1.4 covers.
Lencho measures the damage against a plague of locusts; the item tests recognition of that figurative yardstick, so C-E1.4 rather than LO-1 retrieval.
The narrator states outright that their only hope was the help of God; the answer is lifted from the text, so LO-1.
The method - writing a letter to God - is a narrated action, so information extraction rather than character analysis.
The sum requested (a hundred pesos) is quoted in the letter. LO-1.
The postman's laughter on seeing the address is a narrated event; LO-1 rather than LO-2, because no judgement about him is required.
